I'm checking whether the hit's push, which lands near rotor height and slightly below the robot's centre, would tip us over, and estimating the resulting spin energy against the energy needed to roll over. I'll still make the robot invertible to be safe.

I'm checking whether an invertible build is worth it: a horizontal rotor still fits the height limit, and the extra 3 kg buys protection against flippers, though the rotor's height changes once the robot is upside down. I also need to account for the motor's stall torque reacting back onto the chassis, which at around 214 N·m could work against our grip.

I'm checking whether the wheels can resist the motor's reaction torque of about 214 N·m, since grip only brakes the turn while the wheels are rolling, so the heading controller will have to make up the rest. I'm checking the low-profile option: at about 0.15 m of body height, the wedges that reach the rotor band would catch on the rotor before they could slide under us, and the heavier frame gives a higher moment of inertia against being flipped.

I'm settling the clearance at 8 mm, which keeps the inverted rotor band just under the lowest point where an enemy body could clear it, so it still catches them whichever way we're facing.

I'm comparing a low, wide chassis (0.8 by 0.85 m, 0.15 m tall) against the earlier design, since it keeps the volume at about 0.1 m³ and gives the wheels more leverage for turning.

I'm recalculating the mass budget for the low, wide chassis: frame, electronics, drive, and the spinner together come to about 82 kg, leaving roughly 21 kg for armor.

I'm working out whether a steel front plate would do better than the wedge: the rotor would take about 30% of each hit, roughly 7 kJ per impact, which could wear down their weapon over several hits.

I'm checking whether the unabsorbed energy from a wedge hit goes straight into the robot's structure, and I'm weighing the plate's leak risk against the wedge's cell-by-cell wear.

I'm settling the wedge's thickness at 14mm, since that keeps the plate from wearing through on typical hits. I'm also questioning whether the tank's mass and geometry change the energy figures, and I'm watching for hits on the sides and back.

I'm checking the side wedges and the chassis mass budget, since four wedges at 14mm would be too heavy. Thinner side wedges would leak past their absorption limit, so I'm looking at how the chassis height affects the mass budget.

I'm weighing whether to keep the chassis small with a 0.7 m wedge or go bigger, and whether taller sides would raise the centre too much. On the judging side, the wear to their rotor doesn't count as damage I've dealt, so that part won't help my score.

I'm checking the control side now: their 4mm tip can slide under my 14mm tip in a front-to-front meeting, so I could end up riding up. Last round I spent about 2.1 s riding up versus their 3.9 s, which seems acceptable.

I'm sizing up the scoring now: I need about a half-point lead on points, and if they pick up damage on me the margin flips. Keeping their damage near zero means my armour has to hold up over roughly fifty hits, so I'm considering whether I need a weapon of my own as well.

I'm looking at the opponent's underside, which has no armour, so a flipper could get under them. A flipper plate just above the floor should slide under even their front wedge, and I'm estimating how high a throw from about 2.8 kJ would send their robot.

Now I'm adding up the mass for a 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.28 m chassis: about 74.8 kg including the 14 mm front wedge, which leaves roughly 35 kg for side and back armour and a flipper. Next I'm weighing how the side and back defences would fit into that remaining budget.

I'm comparing wedge mass against protection: a shorter wedge at a steeper angle gives the same protection per kilogram, since the mass scales with length and the deflection scales with the sine of the angle.

I'm noting that a steeper, thinner wedge gives the same protection per kilogram as a shallow one, and that a 45° wedge beats a flat side plate of the same height. I'm also considering whether an upward push from a steep wedge could flip their robot, which would count as wedge damage for me.

Now I'm checking whether a flipper can fit into the budget, since the remaining 35 kg has to cover armour, wedges and the flipper itself. The steel wedges would each come out to about 4.5 kg, which is thinner than the minimum plate thickness, so I'm weighing how much of that budget a flipper should take.

I'm also considering trimming the front wedge to 12 mm, which would lower its mass to about 35 kg and still keep the raw energy threshold around 22.7 kJ.

I'm working through how the 12 mm front wedge would hold up over many hits, since a lower thickness cuts the mass but the wear on each cell adds up across the round.

I'm checking whether the rotor loses enough energy after a hit that later strikes hit weaker, and estimating its self-damage per hit against its total health to see how many hits it could survive before it dies.

I'm weighing side protection as the priority, since a single hit to the sides or back could leak a meaningful share of the energy past the armour, and I'd be losing on damage from just a couple of those.

Now I'm weighing how many hits a thinner front wedge can take before leaks start, and I'm trying a 10 mm wedge, which would cost about 29.8 kg.

I'm checking whether a narrower front wedge at 0.6 × 0.5 m, or a smaller footprint with a taller chassis, would save mass. Either way the perimeter stays about the same, so the saving is negligible.

I'm checking the centre-height geometry: the hit sits about 0.1 m below the centre, so the turning impulse on a wedge hit is roughly 12 Ns, which works out to an angular speed of about 3.2 rad/s and roughly 20 J of rotational energy.

I'm checking whether the rotor's hit height stays within the wedge's coverage, and I'm settling on a 12° wedge that runs the full 0.6 m, since I'm betting the opponent's rotor height won't shift much.

I'm settling on the option of keeping the body low, since raising it above the rotor's reach isn't possible: the top of the chassis would still sit above the rotor's band, so that route is ruled out.

I'm considering a small flipper, but at about 5.6 kg it would only help if I ended up upside down, which seems unlikely, so I'm leaning toward skipping it and building a pure wedge design. The real route to winning is either judging on aggression or wearing down their rotor, and their robot seems to back off to spin up before striking, so I'm planning to keep chasing them constantly.

I'm estimating the expected score now: about 6.5 for me against 4.5 for them, but if they leak around 0.4 through my armour, it drops to a draw. So I need to keep the leak under roughly 15 kJ. I'm also considering whether to thicken the side wedges a little by taking from the front, since front hits have been the only kind landing so far.
